title: Homer & The Longing Worth Suffering to Satisfy
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: In the second essay of his series on Homer, written as part of a three-year reading plan through primary sources in philosophy, literature, history and theology, Colton Cauthen turns from the Iliad to the Odyssey and its theme of home and family. He notes that Odysseus, stranded with the goddess Calypso on a paradisal island, sits weeping for home rather than enjoying immortality and pleasure. Drawing on the Fagles translation, he shows that Odysseus longs not only for Penelope but for his house, land, country and parents, so that Homer's vision of the household is larger than a modern romance. Cauthen contrasts this with the modern saying that home is where the heart is, which defines home purely by individual feeling, and argues that homes, like gardens, decay without someone to maintain and order them. He closes by linking the Odyssey to C.S. Lewis's longing for a real country in The Weight of Glory and The Last Battle.
points: Reading Homer directly rather than reading about him lets the Odyssey challenge modern assumptions, here about what home is worth.
Odysseus rejects immortality and a goddess for the sake of home, showing that Homer treats home as a good worth years of suffering.
Homer's idea of home covers the whole household, including parents, son, land and country, not only the marriage.
The modern slogan that home is where the heart is makes home portable and subjective, whereas the epic treats it as stability, order and inheritance that must be defended and maintained.
The essay connects Odysseus's longing to Lewis's "real country," suggesting earthly homesickness points toward a deeper home.
quotes: Only, they weep not at what is trivial, but at that which is genuinely moving. What was it, then, that kept Odysseus forlorn, despite his otherwise idealistic conditions?
It’s worth noting that Odysseus’ driving motivation is not merely, perhaps not even primarily, returning to his lovely wife, Penelope, but also returning to his house, land, country, and parents.
This is one of my favorite lines from the whole book. He exalts the vision of family in which a man and woman unite, possessing their home in harmony, working together as one

Like Achilles, Odysseus’ weeping is a sort of bracket around the epic. Unlike Achilles, Odysseus weeps at first over something of great value that has been lost, and at last because that which was lost has now been found.
Maybe in our excitement over mobility and opportunity, we have lost a vision for the great stability, order, meaning, and value that home provides.

Home is not ultimately defined by any externalities like history, tradition, geography, or community. It is defined entirely by the individual, based on their internal emotions and sense of well-being.
Homes, like gardens and every other beautiful thing, do not stay beautiful without someone to maintain them and establish order.
In his works, Lewis points all of us to a real country— a real home— that we long to reach and that makes the journey there worthwhile, sufferings and all.
